sentences.text: Megalneusaurus is a large pliosaurid plesiosaur, a member of the large-headed, short-necked pliosauromorph morphotype, classified as a distinct genus.

Most recent estimates suggest the animal was between 7.6 and 9.2 meters long, though a 2024 study estimated it at approximately 9.8 meters with a body mass of 12 tons, reaching a size comparable to Liopleurodon.
It possessed four flippers, an elongated head, and a short neck, with longer hind limbs than forelimbs, suggesting it was a thalassophonean-like pliosaurid.

The rear flippers were larger than the front flippers, with aspect ratios of 8.0 and at least 8.2 respectively, suggesting the animal could move quickly and nimbly, albeit inefficiently, to capture prey.
The hind limbs of the holotype suffered from avascular necrosis, a condition scientists suggest resulted from ascending too quickly after deep dives.
Wilbur Clinton Knight initially identified the flippers of the holotype specimen as hind limbs in 1895, a conclusion confirmed by the discovery of a third flipper in 2008.

Wilbur Clinton Knight discovered the fossils near the town of Ervay, Wyoming, in 1895. He first described the animal as a species of Cimoliosaurus before elevating it to its own genus in 1898, concluding the fossils belonged to a pliosaur.
Two bone fragments were collected in 1922 by prospector Jack Mason and received by W. R. Smith of the United States Geological Survey.
Megalneusaurus used its flippers for a swimming method known as subaqueous flight, using its flippers as hydrofoils.

Based on stomach contents, it fed on cephalopods and fish, though it likely fed on contemporary plesiosaurs, particularly juveniles or subadults. Massare and colleagues interpreted it as an opportunistic apex predator in the Sundance Formation.
The hind limbs of the holotype suffered from avascular necrosis, a condition scientists suggest resulted from ascending too quickly after deep dives.
The type species of the genus is Megalneusaurus rex. Benson and Druckenmiller named the clade Thalassophonea within Pliosauridae in 2013.

A specimen from southern Alaska dates to the Oxfordian and Kimmeridgian stages of the Late Jurassic, between 156 and 152 million years ago. Megalneusaurus fossils are found in Oxfordian-aged rocks of the Redwater Shale Member of the Sundance Formation. An Alaskan specimen likely comes from Oxfordian to Kimmeridgian rocks of the Snug Harbor Siltstone Member of the Naknek Formation.
The Alaskan specimen suggests that Megalneusaurus occupied colder waters with less diverse fauna.

Some paleontologists consider the genus dubious due to the loss of most fossils, while others maintain its validity. Wahl and colleagues reclassified the Alaskan specimen as M. rex in 2010, though some authors remain doubtful about its attribution to the genus. In 2003, Ellis noted that many researchers doubted the diagnostic value of the holotype due to lost fossils, while others held the opposite opinion.
